title: Kohlhaas v. State
description: Whether Alaska's Initiative 2, which implemented an open nonpartisan primary and ranked-choice voting, violates political parties' associational rights, the constitutional provisions for electing the lieutenant governor, or the constitutional provisions for electing the governor.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Initiative 2 infringed on political parties' associational rights by altering the primary system and allowing candidates to list party affiliation without endorsement, violated the constitutional method for nominating the lieutenant governor by pairing candidates, and unconstitutionally burdened the right to vote by adopting ranked-choice voting which they claimed required a majority or denied victory to the first-round plurality winner.
defendant_argument: The defendants contended that Initiative 2 did not burden associational rights as it decoupled state elections from party nominations and included disclaimers, that it complied with the constitutional provisions for the lieutenant governor by allowing joint tickets and flexible nomination methods, and that ranked-choice voting was a single tabulation process that did not require a majority to win and served important regulatory interests without unconstitutionally burdening the right to vote.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the superior court's judgment, ruling that Initiative 2 is constitutional and does not violate the Alaska Constitution.

title: State Department of Education & Early Development v. Alexander
description: Whether Alaska statutes permitting public funds for correspondence study programs, which can be used for private school tuition, violate the state constitution's prohibition against direct benefits to religious or other private educational institutions.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff (Alexander) argued that the statutes allowing public funds for correspondence study, particularly for private school tuition, are facially unconstitutional or unconstitutional as applied, violating the state constitution's prohibition against direct benefits to private educational institutions.
defendant_argument: The defendant (State Department of Education) argued that the statutes are facially constitutional because they have a "plainly legitimate sweep" with many valid uses of funds, even if some applications (like private school tuition) might be unconstitutional. Intervenor-appellants (Moceri) argued that the benefit to private schools is indirect and thus permissible.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the superior court's judgment, ruling that the allotment and ILP statutes are not facially unconstitutional and remanding the case for further proceedings, declining to rule on the constitutionality of using funds for private school tuition at this stage.

title: Valoaga v. State
description: Whether the Department of Corrections (DOC) violated an inmate's due process rights by using a preponderance of the evidence standard in disciplinary proceedings and by not offering an alternative saliva test for drug screening.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that DOC must prove prison rule violations by clear and convincing evidence, not a preponderance of the evidence, and that failing to offer a saliva test when he could not urinate violated his due process rights.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the Alaska Constitution permits the use of a preponderance of the evidence standard in prison disciplinary proceedings and that the plaintiff's argument regarding saliva tests was not preserved for review.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's decision, ruling that the preponderance of the evidence standard is constitutional for prison disciplinary proceedings and that the argument regarding alternative saliva tests was waived.

title: Alaska Trappers Association v. City of Valdez
description: Whether a city ordinance limiting trapping in certain areas is preempted by state law, with the plaintiff arguing it is preempted by state authority over natural resources, and the defendant arguing it is a valid exercise of local home rule authority for public safety and land use.
plaintiff_argument: The city's ordinance limiting trapping is preempted by state law, violates AS 16.05.790, and article VIII of the Alaska Constitution, as the state has pervasive authority over natural resources and the Board of Game has sole authority over trapping.
defendant_argument: The city has constitutional and statutory authority as a home rule municipality to regulate land use and public safety, and its ordinance is not expressly or impliedly prohibited by state law, as its impact on wildlife management is incidental.
decision_outcome: The superior court's order granting summary judgment to the City of Valdez was affirmed, concluding that the city's ordinance is not prohibited by the Alaska Constitution or the legislature's delegation of authority over fish and game to the Board.

title: State v. McKelvey
description: Whether police must obtain a warrant before taking pictures of a person's yard with a zoom lens from an airplane, with the State arguing it is permissible due to common air travel and public visibility, and the respondent arguing it constitutes an unreasonable search under the Alaska Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that because small airplane travel is common in Alaska and any passenger might peer into a yard, law enforcement officials may do the same without a warrant.
defendant_argument: McKelvey argued that the warrantless observation of his home with a telephoto lens during a flight constituted an illegal search under the Alaska Constitution.
decision_outcome: The Alaska Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, holding that law enforcement officials must obtain a warrant before using aircraft and vision-enhancing technology to observe the curtilage of a person's home that is protected from ground-level observation.

title: Vazquez v. State
description: Whether Jennie Armstrong met the three-year Alaska residency requirement to be eligible to serve in the legislature by the June 1, 2022 filing deadline.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Liz Vazquez, argued that Jennie Armstrong did not establish Alaska residency until June 7, 2019, at the earliest, making her ineligible to hold public office.
defendant_argument: The defendant, Jennie Armstrong, argued that she became an Alaska resident on May 20, 2019, thereby meeting the three-year residency requirement by the filing deadline.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's decision that Jennie Armstrong met the constitutional requirements, including the three-year state residency requirement, for serving in the legislature.

title: Native Village of Kwinhagak v. State, Department of Health & Social Services
description: Whether the Office of Children's Services (OCS) must follow civil commitment statutes when admitting a child in its custody to a hospital for psychiatric treatment, and whether a 46-day hospitalization without a prompt hearing violates the child's constitutional due process rights.
plaintiff_argument: The Native Village of Kwinhagak argued that OCS must follow civil commitment statutes for psychiatric hospitalization and that the prolonged hospitalization without a prompt hearing violated the child's constitutional due process rights.
defendant_argument: The State of Alaska argued that OCS has authority under CINA statutes to admit children to psychiatric care, not civil commitment statutes, and that existing injunctions provided sufficient procedural protections.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the superior court's order, ruling that OCS was not required to follow civil commitment statutes for psychiatric hospitalization but that the 46-day delay in holding a hearing violated the child's procedural due process rights.

title: Sitka Tribe of Alaska v. State
description: Whether the Alaska Department of Fish and Game has a constitutional duty to provide all relevant information to the Board of Fisheries for resource management decisions, whether the Sitka Tribe of Alaska faced irreparable harm warranting a preliminary injunction, and whether the Tribe was the prevailing party for attorney's fees.
plaintiff_argument: The Sitka Tribe argued that the Alaska Constitution requires the Department to provide all relevant information to the Board, that they faced irreparable harm justifying a preliminary injunction against the Department's fishery management interpretation, and that they were the prevailing party for attorney's fees due to their success on statutory claims.
defendant_argument: The State and Alliance argued there is no constitutional duty for the Department to provide all relevant information, that the Tribe did not demonstrate irreparable harm for an injunction, and that the constitutional claim was a main issue, thus the Tribe was not the sole prevailing party for attorney's fees.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the superior court's decisions, denying the Tribe's constitutional claim, denying the preliminary injunction, and denying attorney's fees to all parties, while acknowledging the Tribe's prior success on statutory and regulatory claims.

title: Taylor v. Alaska Legislative Affairs Agency
description: Whether the Alaska Constitution bars a lawsuit brought by the Alaska Attorney General against the Legislative Affairs Agency, specifically concerning the effective date of an appropriations bill.
plaintiff_argument: Attorney General Taylor argued that his lawsuit was not constitutionally barred, asserting common law authority distinct from the governor's and that prior case law (Knowles) allowed challenges to non-legislative acts.
defendant_argument: The Legislative Affairs Agency argued that the Alaska Constitution's Article III, Section 16, bars the Attorney General's suit because his authority is substantively the same as the governor's, and the suit was, in essence, against the legislature.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the superior court's decision, ruling that Attorney General Taylor's suit was unconstitutional and barred by Article III, Section 16 of the Alaska Constitution.

title: Williams Alaska Petroleum, Inc. v. State
description: Whether Williams Alaska Petroleum, Inc. is strictly liable for sulfolane and PFAS contamination, associated damages, and remediation costs, and whether the superior court's decision violated Williams's due process rights or constituted an unconstitutional taking.
plaintiff_argument: The State and Flint Hills argued that Williams is strictly liable for sulfolane and PFAS releases, that sulfolane is a hazardous substance, and that Williams must pay damages, response costs, and contribute to remediation.
defendant_argument: Williams argued that sulfolane is not a hazardous substance, that the awarded damages and costs were erroneous, that the injunctive and declaratory relief was improper, that the purchase agreement was misinterpreted regarding liability allocation, and that the decision violated due process and constituted an unconstitutional taking.
decision_outcome: The court largely affirmed the superior court's decision, concluding that Williams is strictly liable for sulfolane and PFAS releases, awarding response costs and natural resource damages to the State and Flint Hills, and affirming contribution awards, but remanded the injunctive relief for more specificity.

title: In re Abigail B.
description: Whether the lengthy delays between individuals' pre-evaluation detentions and their transportation to an evaluation facility violated their substantive due process rights.
plaintiff_argument: Abigail and Jethro argued that their prolonged pre-evaluation detentions violated their substantive due process rights because the nature and duration of the detentions were not reasonably related to the purpose of facilitating immediate transportation for evaluation.
defendant_argument: The State argued that broader purposes for pre-evaluation detention, such as protecting vulnerable individuals and society, justified the detentions, and that the detentions were reasonably related to these broader purposes.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the superior court orders that authorized the continued pre-evaluation detention of Abigail and Jethro following their review hearings.

title: In re 2021 Redistricting Cases
description: Whether the Alaska Redistricting Board's legislative district plans, specifically Senate District K and the Cantwell Appendage in House District 36, are constitutional under Alaska's equal protection, due process, and redistricting requirements, or if they constitute unconstitutional gerrymandering and violate public hearing mandates.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the Board's redistricting plans, including Senate District K and the Cantwell Appendage in House District 36, were unconstitutional due to partisan gerrymandering, lack of compactness, insufficient socioeconomic integration, and violations of public hearing and due process requirements.
defendant_argument: The Board argued its redistricting plans complied with constitutional requirements for compactness, contiguity, and socioeconomic integration, that it followed proper procedures, and that the superior court erred in its findings of unconstitutional gerrymandering, due process violations, and public hearing failures.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed that Senate District K and the Cantwell Appendage in House District 36 were unconstitutional gerrymanders, reversed the superior court's 'hard look' analysis for House Districts 3 and 4, and ordered the Board to adopt an interim plan for the 2022 elections while remanding for a final constitutional plan.

title: Knolmayer v. McCollum
description: Whether Alaska Statute 09.55.548(b), which reduces medical malpractice awards by collateral source compensation, violates the equal protection clause of the Alaska Constitution when applied to claimants whose insurers have contractual reimbursement rights.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that AS 09.55.548(b) should not apply to her case because her ERISA-governed health plan falls under the "federal program" exception, or that ERISA preempts the statute, or that the statute creates an unconstitutional "double deduction" and violates equal protection.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that AS 09.55.548(b) is not preempted by ERISA, that the Lowe's Plan is not a "federal program" exception, and that the statute's purpose is to reduce malpractice awards by preventing double recoveries or shifting the burden of loss to the injured person.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that AS 09.55.548(b) does not apply to ERISA plans as a "federal program" exception, and that ERISA does not preempt the statute. However, the court found that AS 09.55.548(b) violates the Alaska Constitution's equal protection clause when applied to claimants whose insurers have a contractual right to reimbursement, because it creates an unfair distinction among malpractice claimants and does not fairly relate to the purpose of preventing double recoveries. The superior court's order of April 30, 2020, was vacated and remanded.

title: Short v. State
description: Whether the Higher Education Investment Fund (HEIF) is subject to the state's annual budgetary "sweep" provision, with the students arguing it is not sweepable due to prior appropriation and the Executive Branch arguing it is sweepable under constitutional provisions and precedent.
plaintiff_argument: The students argued that the HEIF is not sweepable because its appropriations do not lapse and the funds have already been validly appropriated and expended for investments. They also contended that making the HEIF sweepable would violate the separation of powers and that the controlling precedent, Cowper, was erroneous and should be overturned.
defendant_argument: The Executive Branch argued that the HEIF is sweepable under existing case law (Hickel v. Cowper) and the plain language of Article IX, Section 17 of the Alaska Constitution, because further legislative appropriations are required for its expenditure. They maintained that the sweep is a constitutional mandate and does not violate the separation of powers.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Alaska affirmed the superior court's decision, ruling that the Higher Education Investment Fund (HEIF) is sweepable under the state's constitutional provisions.

title: Department of Corrections v. Stefano
description: Whether the superior court has appellate jurisdiction to review the Department of Corrections' (DOC) decision to remove an inmate from electronic monitoring, and whether DOC's decision implicates the inmate's constitutional rights to due process and rehabilitation.
plaintiff_argument: Stefano argued that his removal from electronic monitoring violated his constitutional rights to due process and rehabilitation, and that the superior court had appellate jurisdiction to review DOC's decision because it involved fundamental constitutional rights and an adjudicative record.
defendant_argument: The Department of Corrections (DOC) argued that the superior court lacked appellate jurisdiction to review its decision, that electronic monitoring is not a formal rehabilitative program, and that its decision to remove Stefano did not implicate a fundamental constitutional right to rehabilitation or produce an adjudicative record for review.
decision_outcome: The court held that serving a sentence on electronic monitoring affords a limited but constitutionally protected degree of liberty, requiring due process for removal. However, the court also held that the superior court lacked appellate jurisdiction to review DOC's decision in this case because DOC's decisional process was not an adjudicative proceeding and did not create an adequate record for appellate review. The court vacated the superior court's decision and remanded the case to be converted into a civil action for judicial review.

title: State v. The Alaska Legislative Council
description: Whether forward funding for public education, which appropriates funds for future fiscal years, is consistent with the annual budgeting process established by the Alaska Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The Alaska Legislative Council and Coalition for Education Equity argued that forward-funded appropriations for public education were consistent with the legislature's constitutional authority and did not violate any specific constitutional provision, and that the governor's refusal to disburse funds violated his duty to faithfully execute the laws.
defendant_argument: The State of Alaska, Governor Mike Dunleavy, argued that forward funding violated the annual appropriations model established by the Alaska Constitution, infringing on the governor's veto power and the prohibition on dedicating revenues.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the superior court's decision, concluding that forward-funded appropriations are unconstitutional and vacated the attorney's fees awards.

title: State v. Graham
description: Whether the Court of Appeals erred in vacating Stacey Graham's sentence and remanding for resentencing before a different judge, specifically regarding the application of sentencing standards and the admissibility of victim impact evidence.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the superior court properly applied sentencing standards and that the admission of police testimony and victim tribute videos did not warrant vacating the sentence or requiring a different judge for resentencing.
defendant_argument: Graham argued his sentence was excessive due to errors in applying sentencing benchmarks, improper reliance on aggravating factors, and the improper admission of emotionally charged victim impact evidence (police testimony and tribute videos), which necessitated resentencing by a different judge.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, vacated Graham's sentence, and remanded for resentencing by the same judge, finding errors in the admission of police officer testimony and victim tribute videos (without prior review) but no errors in the sentencing standards applied by the superior court or the need for judge recusal.

title: Association of Village Council Presidents Regional Housing Authority v. Mael
description: Whether the housing authority owed a tort duty to inspect the boiler with reasonable care, and whether the statutory noneconomic damages cap was constitutionally applied to the plaintiff's award and other family members' emotional distress damages.
plaintiff_argument: The housing authority had an independent tort duty to inspect the boiler with reasonable care, and its negligence caused the explosion. The statutory damages cap, as applied, violates due process because it fails to account for inflation and the severe nature of Dietrich's injuries, and the family members' NIED damages should not be aggregated under the same cap.
defendant_argument: The housing authority had no tort duty to inspect the boiler at the time of the explosion, as any contractual duty had expired. The explosion was caused by a product defect, not negligent inspection. All noneconomic damages, including those for family members' emotional distress, should be aggregated under a single statutory cap, and the cap is constitutional.
decision_outcome: The superior court's judgment is affirmed, upholding that the housing authority had a tort duty to inspect the boiler, that the jury's finding of negligence was supported by evidence, and that the statutory damages cap was properly applied to Dietrich's noneconomic damages but not aggregated with the family members' emotional distress damages.

title: Dutchess v. Dutch
description: Whether the superior court erred in granting the father sole legal custody to make vaccination decisions for their minor children, despite the mother's religious objections and claims of constitutional violations.
plaintiff_argument: The mother argued that granting the father sole legal custody for vaccination decisions infringed upon her constitutional right to free exercise of religion and violated her due process rights.
defendant_argument: The father argued that vaccinating the children was in their best interests, as recommended by their pediatrician, and sought sole legal custody for vaccination decisions.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's order, granting the father sole legal authority to make vaccination decisions for the children.

title: Sagoonick v. State
description: Whether the State of Alaska's resource development policies, which contribute to climate change, violate the constitutional rights of young Alaskans to a stable climate system and protection of natural resources.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the State's resource development policies and actions contribute to climate change, violating their fundamental constitutional rights to a stable climate system, life, liberty, property, and equal protection, breaching the public trust doctrine, and that the Department's denial of their rulemaking petition was unconstitutional.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the superior court correctly dismissed the lawsuit because injunctive relief claims presented non-justiciable political questions, declaratory relief claims should be left for actual controversies, and the Department's denial of the rulemaking petition complied with statutory requirements, as resource management is a legislative function.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's dismissal of the plaintiffs' lawsuit, ruling against the plaintiffs' claims for injunctive and declaratory relief regarding climate change and resource development.

title: Department of Administration v. Retired Public Employees of Alaska, Inc.
description: Whether the State's 2014 revision of the dental insurance plan for public retirees unconstitutionally diminished accrued benefits, and whether the analysis of diminishment should include the premium rates paid by retirees.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the 2014 dental plan diminished retirees' accrued benefits and that the premiums paid by retirees are irrelevant to the diminishment analysis.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the dental plan was not an accrued benefit, or if it was, the court erred by not considering premium rates in the diminishment analysis.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the superior court's judgment and remanded the case for a new diminishment analysis that includes consideration of premium rates, while affirming that the option to purchase dental insurance is an accrued benefit.

title: Dunleavy v. Alaska Legislative Council ex rel. Alaska State Legislature
description: Whether the Alaska Legislature's statutory provisions defining legislative inaction on gubernatorial appointments as a constructive rejection violate the Alaska Constitution's requirement for a joint session vote for confirmation or rejection.
plaintiff_argument: The Legislative Council argued that AS 39.05.080(3) and H.B. 309, which define legislative inaction as a declination of confirmation, are constitutional and that the governor's appointees were therefore lawfully rejected.
defendant_argument: The Governor argued that AS 39.05.080(3) and H.B. 309 violate Article III, Sections 25 and 26 of the Alaska Constitution, which require an affirmative joint session vote to confirm or reject appointees, and thus his appointees remained in office.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the superior court's judgment, concluding that the laws defining legislative inaction as a rejection of gubernatorial appointees violate the Alaska Constitution.

title: State v. Arctic Village Council
description: Whether the absentee ballot witness requirement unconstitutionally burdened the right to vote during the COVID-19 pandemic.
plaintiff_argument: The witness requirement unconstitutionally burdened the right to vote during the COVID-19 pandemic, forcing voters to choose between risking their health or foregoing their right to vote, especially for vulnerable individuals and those in communities with strict social distancing.
defendant_argument: The witness requirement was necessary for deterring voter fraud and promoting voter confidence in the election's integrity, and the plaintiffs waited too long to file suit.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's decision to grant a preliminary injunction, suspending the absentee ballot witness requirement for the 2020 general election.

title: State v. Recall Dunleavy
description: Whether the recall application against Governor Dunleavy met the legal and factual sufficiency requirements to be presented to the voters.
plaintiff_argument: The recall committee argued that their application, citing lack of fitness, incompetence, and neglect of duties, was legally and factually sufficient for recall.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the recall application was not legally or factually sufficient, and that the grounds for recall should be narrowly defined, not allowing for purely political recalls.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's decision, finding that the recall application, with one minor exception, satisfied the legal requirements for presentation to the voters.

title: State v. Galvin
description: Whether the Division of Elections' ballot design, which omitted a candidate's nonpartisan voter registration, violated statutory requirements and the candidate's right to free political association under the Alaska Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Alyse Galvin argued that the Division of Elections' ballot design, which omitted her nonpartisan voter registration, violated a statutory directive to designate a candidate's party affiliation on the ballot and her right to free political association.
defendant_argument: The Division of Elections argued that its ballot design was permissible, that 'party affiliation' and 'party designation' were synonymous, and that granting a preliminary injunction to change the ballots would jeopardize the prospects of a successful and timely election.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's denial of Alyse Galvin's requested preliminary injunction, ruling that granting it would imperil the public interest in an orderly and timely election.

title: Watson v. State
description: Whether the statute that excludes misdemeanor traffic violations from juvenile court jurisdiction violates a minor's right to equal protection under the Alaska Constitution, with the plaintiff arguing it is unfair to treat misdemeanor DUI offenders as adults while felony DUI offenders are treated as juveniles, and the defendant arguing the statute is constitutional as driving is an adult activity and it promotes public safety while protecting juveniles from harsh felony consequences.
plaintiff_argument: Elizabeth Watson argued that the statute requiring her to be prosecuted in district court as an adult for misdemeanor DUI, rather than in juvenile court, deprived her of equal protection under the law, as it unfairly differs from dispositions for other misdemeanors in the juvenile code and treats felony DUI offenses differently.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the legislature could reasonably decide to treat misdemeanor traffic violations consistently to promote public safety, as driving is an adult activity, and that the statute also reasonably protects juvenile offenders from the harsh collateral consequences of a felony conviction by allowing felony traffic offenses into juvenile court.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Alaska affirmed the judgment of the district court, concluding that the statute is constitutional and does not violate the equal protection clause.

title: Metcalfe v. State
description: Whether the repeal of a statutory provision allowing former state employees to reinstate their credited service and original benefits tier upon re-employment and repayment of withdrawn contributions diminished or impaired an accrued benefit of the retirement system, protected by Article XII, Section 7 of the Alaska Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the statutory right to reinstate credited service was an accrued benefit protected by Article XII, Section 7 of the Alaska Constitution, and its repeal unconstitutionally diminished that benefit.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the reinstatement right was not an accrued benefit protected by the constitution, as it was an employment benefit, not a membership benefit, and only applied to active members, not former members, and was merely an offer that could be revoked.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the superior court's summary judgment order, ruling that the statutory reinstatement right was an accrued benefit protected by the constitution and its repeal was unconstitutional.
